*Version 0.9 · 27 November 2026*

## Who is this course for?

You are a social scientist: a sociologist, a political scientist, an anthropologist, an economist. You have used ChatGPT or Claude in a browser, mostly to improve a text or as a better search engine. You haven't used it for the actual work of your field, and you may never have written a line of code. This course is for you. Seniority doesn't matter.

When I say you should **experiment** with agentic AI, I hear two typical reactions.

*"This is for coders."* It isn't. You won't type a single command. You give instructions in plain language, as you would to a research assistant. Even the technical setup is done by the agent, which explains each step before it takes it.

*"I don't need this."* Maybe. The course lets you find out on your own material. You remain in charge, and you decide how much to delegate. You will see what an agent can do and how to supervise it. At the very least, you get a glimpse.

We use one tool: **Claude Code, in the Claude desktop app**, on Windows, Mac or Linux. Codex by OpenAI is the most similar, and what you learn here carries over fully. Antigravity, with Google's Gemini, is also similar, and there are close alternatives that run open-weights models. But when learning, one tool is enough.

## What is an AI agent?

Let's start with what you know. **A chatbot** is a conversation in a browser. You paste in a text or upload a file, it answers, and you copy the answer back into your document. It knows only what you gave it in that conversation. It mostly relies on information it "remembers" from its training, which can be wrong. It cannot read your files, run code, or save results.

**An agent** is the same AI model with four additions. First, it has access to **folders** on your computer: the ones you allow. Second, it can **act** there: open files, write and run program code, save results. Third, it works in a **loop**: it takes a step, looks at the result and decides on the next one, until the task is done or it needs you. Fourth, it can **use tools**: open a browser, or call other programs such as Microsoft Word.

The loop makes the difference. Suppose you ask for *a chart of turnout by age group from survey.csv*. A chatbot needs the file uploaded and may guess what the columns mean. The agent does the following:

1. it opens the file and sees that age is called `age_cat`, not `age`;
2. it writes a short program and runs it;
3. it hits an error because some ages are coded "refused", and asks you how to handle them (or makes an assumption you can check);
4. it runs the program again, opens the chart to check it, and saves it in `output/`.

You see every step, and at first it asks your permission before each one.

It helps to **think of the agent as a very fast research assistant sitting at your computer**. It has read a lot, but it is new to your project, and it can be wrong with confidence. Hence your job shifts from doing each step to instructing the agent and checking its work. Checking matters most.

One more point changes how you use it. The model behind the agent is not a database. It doesn't look facts up in its memory, it reconstructs them, so a reference, a number or a date it "remembers" can be wrong. It is much stronger at working with material you put in front of it. So working with an agent is largely about designing its context: you provide the grounding material (your readings, your data, your notes) and the tools to search and compute, and you ask it to work from those rather than from memory. A table of readings built from the PDFs in your folder can be checked line by line. One built from what the model recalls cannot.

Indeed, the right habit is to make it write code that can be run directly, and notes that can be searched directly.

## What can it do for a social scientist?

Here are a few tasks that fit an agent well. None of them needs you to write code.

:::: {.uses}
::: {.use}
**Hundreds of historical notes, as OCR-ed PDFs.** Many large PDFs in a folder first become plain text, which can then be searched and turned into a data table.
:::

::: {.use}
**A draft in Word.** The agent comments on the argument, or edits a copy, and you review each edit as a tracked change.
:::

::: {.use}
**Paper review.** A detailed review of a draft, with agents that check the numbers, the references and the argument. The agent reads the literature, places your work in it, and suggests journals.
:::

::: {.use}
**Data analysis.** The agent downloads data, cleans it, runs regressions, makes tables and charts, and writes a first-pass report that describes the data. You check the code and the results.
:::

::: {.use}
**Prototype.** You have an idea. The agent does the first pass: literature, data, code and a draft. Then you decide whether it is worth your time to continue.
:::
::::

The agent has limits, too. First, the agent makes mistakes, and it makes them in fluent, confident prose. It may misread a variable, drop observations without telling you, or hand you a paraphrase in quotation marks. Second, it doesn't know the judgment calls of your field: which cases belong in the sample, or what a concept means in your literature. Third, what it reads is sent to the company's servers, so confidential material needs care.

Each of these problems has a routine that handles it, and you already know most of them from supervising research assistants and refereeing papers. Part 2 builds them into every step.

## Worried you will break something?

Many people are, and it is a good instinct. Here is why you can relax.

- **Nothing happens without your click.** In Manual mode, where we start, the agent asks before it changes a file or runs anything. When in doubt, click **Deny**. Nothing bad follows from a deny.
- **It works in one folder you choose.** Your other files are outside it. If a request ever names another folder, click **Deny** and ask why.
- **Start with copies.** Put copies of your files in the project folder and keep the originals where they are. In the worst case, you delete the folder and start again.
- **You can stop it at any time.** The stop button interrupts it mid-step.
- **You can ask before you allow.** *"What does this do? Is it safe? Can it be undone?"* The agent answers in plain language.
- **You can't run up a bill.** Pro has a fixed monthly price. When you reach the usage limit, the agent pauses until the limit resets, unless you choose to buy extra usage.
- **Even the Python setup can be undone.** The agent writes down what it installed and how to remove all of it ([Step 1.4](setup.qmd#step-1-4)).

## What do you need?

- **A paid Claude plan.** Claude Code needs **Claude Pro** or higher (about \$20 a month, cancel any time; see [pricing](https://claude.com/pricing)). A university Claude Team or Enterprise plan also works. **ChatGPT Plus** includes OpenAI's Codex, the closest alternative. Antigravity, with Google's Gemini, is similar. See [Which plan do I need?](setup.qmd#step-1-1)
- **A computer** with Windows 10 or 11, macOS, or Linux (Ubuntu or Debian).
- **Permission to install software.** A university laptop may need IT approval. Try first, and ask if you are blocked.

## How is the course organized?

The course has six parts and an assignment. The first two parts are hands-on: setup takes about an hour, the first project about two. The third is a live demonstration. The assignment follows it: you read the agent's paper as a referee would, and you improve its prompt with skills. The fourth part is a guide to the weeks after: you make the rules and the skills yours, and you run a project on a question of your own. The fifth is broader advice for later, on other uses and other models. The sixth is a short list of links on where social science research may be heading. If something fails along the way, nothing is broken: check the troubleshooting table of that part, or ask the agent what went wrong.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Taking this as a two-hour workshop?

**Before the session (at home, about an hour):** Part 1, and Step 2.1.

**In the session (two hours):** at the start we give the agent the World Cup prompt of Part 3, and it works in the background. The first hour is Part 2: we explain a few ideas, you work on Steps 2.2 to 2.4 on your own laptop, and we end with a short debrief. The second hour is Part 3: the prompt, what it leaves out, and what the agent produced.

**After the session (homework):** Steps 2.5 and 2.6 of Part 2, and the [Assignment](assignment.qmd) on the World Cup project folder we share. Part 4 is for the weeks after, and Parts 5 and 6 for later.

## A short glossary

- **Agent:** an AI model that acts on your computer (reads files, runs code, saves results) in a loop until a task is done.
- **Prompt:** the instruction you type for the agent. In this course, prompts to copy come in boxes.
- **Session:** one conversation with the agent. Each session starts fresh.
- **Context window:** what the model can see at once. Long sessions fill it up, and quality drops.
- **Permission mode:** how much the agent may do without asking you. We start with *Manual*: it asks every time. Later many people use *Auto*.
- **Markdown (`.md`):** plain text with a few formatting symbols. It is the common language of people and agents.
- **`AGENTS.md`:** your standing instructions, which the agent reads at the start of every session.
- **Skill:** a recipe file the agent follows for one type of task.
- **Terminal:** a text window for typing commands. The agent uses one behind the scenes. You don't have to.
- **Environment:** a word with two meanings in this course. In the app, it is *where* the agent works: on this computer, or elsewhere (Step 1.2). For Python, it is a project's own set of add-ons, usually in a folder called `.venv` (Step 1.4).
- **Harness:** a word you will hear later. It is the program around the model that gives it these abilities. Claude Code is one.

## Useful links

Many people have written about agents for researchers. These are the ones we find most useful for this audience.

**For people who don't code**

- Chris Blattman, [AI for Professionals Who Don't Code](https://claudeblattman.com/). A political economist's guide to running projects, meetings and everyday academic work with an agent.
- Mushtaq Bilal, [A Beginner's Guide to Claude Code for (Non-Technical) Academics](https://velikov-mihail.github.io/ai-econ-wiki/summaries/bilal-beginners-guide/). Written for the humanities and social sciences. The link is a summary; the original is a long post on X.
- Carl Vellotti, [Claude Code for Researchers](https://ccforeveryone.com/guides/claude-code-for-researchers). Interview transcripts, PDFs and field notes, with good advice on verifying quotes.
- Neal Caren, [social-data-analysis](https://github.com/nealcaren/social-data-analysis). Ready-made skills for qualitative and quantitative sociological research, from interview analysis to literature synthesis.

**If you work with data**

- Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham, [Claude Code for Applied Economists](https://markusacademy.substack.com/p/claude-code-for-applied-economists). Eight video episodes, from getting started to verification.
- Scott Cunningham, [Claude Code Changed How I Work](https://causalinf.substack.com/p/claude-code-changed-how-i-work-part). A long series on empirical research with an agent. Some posts are for subscribers.
- Anton Korinek, [AI Agents for Economic Research](https://www.genaiforecon.org/JEL-2025-Aug-AIAgents.pdf) (August 2025). The latest in his series in the *Journal of Economic Literature* on using AI in economic research.
- Mihail Velikov, [AI in Business & Economic Research](https://velikov-mihail.github.io/ai-econ-wiki/). One-page summaries of more than 180 guides and papers.

**Background reading**

- Ethan Mollick, [One Useful Thing](https://www.oneusefulthing.org/). The best running commentary on working with AI.
- Our own list: [suggested readings and resources](../da-knowledge/beyond.qmd).

**Official documentation**

- Claude Code: [desktop app](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop) · [skills](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills) · [AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory) · [data usage](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/data-usage)

**On this site, when you want more**

- [Week 1: LLMs, Harnesses & Setup](../unit1/index.qmd) explains what is behind the chat box, and covers other agents.
- [Week 2: From Raw Data to Report](../unit2/index.qmd) is a full analysis project with an agent.
